new_statements.quote: All Oti-Volta languages are tonal, following the local areal pattern of terracing tone systems. In all the languages, the individual tones within a word are not independently freely variable, but occur in constrained tone patterns, only a few of which are possible for any given segmental word shape. Gurma and Core EOV have three basic tones; the OOV §7.5 languages only two (secondarily developed to three in Kusaal), but the OOV system conceals an underlying three-way distinction.
new_statements.citation: Eddyshaw, David. 2026. Toward Proto-Oti-Volta. Version of 1. Zenodo (record 21729409). xii+ ca. 330 pp. CC-BY 4.0.
new_statements.locator: §2.7 'Tone', p.79; membership of Yare in WOV: ch.2 p.2 ('the subgroup formed by Mampruli, Dagbani, Hanga, Kamara and Yare') and Sources p.viii; also p.3 'All the languages are tonal, of the "register" type, with two or three basic tones.'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. 'All Oti-Volta languages are tonal..' is a family-wide generalisation; Eddyshaw's Yare/Kantosi material is Naden's untoned lexicon, so nothing is observed on Kantosi tone itself. | checker: copies we hold +) opened. Quote verbatim at section 2.7 'Tone', running head '79 Phonology : Tone' (the text), followed by 2.7.1 'Tone in Outer Oti-Volta' (WOV nominal tone patterns H/L/A). 'Yare' occurs 12 times: Sources p.viii 'Nabit, Talni, Dagbani, Yare and Kamara: Naden, lostmarbles31.wixsite.com/aardvarks-lexico'; map legend 'Yare speakers live amidst other communities in northern Ghana'; ch.2 'the subgroup formed by Mampruli, Dagbani, Hanga, Kamara and Yare'…
new_statements.relation_note: Family-level generalisation only: all Oti-Volta languages (a set in which the author explicitly includes Yare, within the Mampruli-Dagbani-Hanga-Kamara-Yare subgroup of Western Oti-Volta) are register-tone languages with terracing; Outer Oti-Volta (incl. WOV) has two basic tones. Yare-specific statements concern only segmental phonology (loss of contrastive glottalisation, nasalisation and tense/lax vowel contrasts, pp.168-169, 245-247). The Yare data he cites carry no tone marking, and nothing is said about stress/accent for Yare.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Generic claim: every Oti-Volta language, hence Yare/Kantosi by membership, is a terraced register-tone language; WOV languages have two basic tones. No word-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Kusaal secondarily three tones; Nõotre tone system innovated; none concerning Yare.
new_statements.identity_note: Eddyshaw's 'Yare' ('Yare speakers live amidst other communities in northern Ghana'; data source 'Nabit, Talni, Dagbani, Yare and Kamara: Naden, lostmarbles31.wixsite.com/aardvarks-lexico') is Naden's Kantosi/Kantoosi (xkt) under its alternative name Yare; not the Mooré-speaking Yarse of Burkina Faso and not Dagaari Dioula [dgd].

sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Phonological content concerns suffix-vowel insertion/regression, velar-suffix loss, glottal/flap allophones of *g in Mampruli/Kusaal/Dagbani etc; Kantosi (YR 'Yaari') appears only in three untoned lexical citations and in the reference list ('First Notes on Yaari (Kantoonsi)', in prep.). The single occurrence of 'tones' (the text) is about another language's reflexes of medial consonants. No tone or stress statement for Kantosi.
